title: Non-overlapping Intervals
directAnswer: This is the classic activity-selection greedy in disguise. Sort by END time, then keep every interval that starts at or after the last kept interval's end. Each kept interval is a 'survivor'; the answer is n − survivors, the number you had to delete. O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the scan.

remember.pattern: Greedy activity selection — sort by END, keep earliest-finishing
remember.formula:
intervals.sort(by end)
kept = 0; prevEnd = -inf
for s, e in intervals:
    if s >= prevEnd: kept += 1; prevEnd = e   # survivor
return n - kept
rules: **Sort by END, not start.** The interval that finishes earliest leaves the most room for the rest — that's the greedy choice that's provably optimal.
Reframe 'minimum removals' as 'maximum keepers': removals = n − maxNonOverlapping. The keep version is the cleaner greedy.
Keep an interval iff `start >= prevEnd`. Touching is allowed: `[1,2]` and `[2,3]` are non-overlapping, so use `>=`.
When intervals overlap, you 'remove' the one that ends later by simply not updating `prevEnd` — keep the earlier finisher.
Initialize `prevEnd` to negative infinity so the first interval is always kept.
whenToUse: Minimum deletions / maximum subset so intervals don't overlap
Any 'erase the fewest to make disjoint' phrasing
antiSignals: You must MERGE overlaps, not remove them → sort by start, sweep (LC 56)
You need the number of rooms / max concurrent → heap / sweep-line (LC 253)
You insert one interval into a sorted list → three-phase sweep (LC 57)
Weighted intervals (each has a value to maximize) → this greedy fails; use DP (Weighted Job Scheduling)
remember.takeaway: Sorting by END is the signature of greedy activity selection: the earliest-finishing interval always leaves maximal room for what follows, so keeping it is never wrong. Flip 'minimum removals' to 'maximum keepers' and the whole problem becomes a one-pass count.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize this as activity selection and sort by END time, instead of sorting by start and trying to reason about which overlapper to delete.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Sorting by start and then deleting greedily — it's tempting but you can't cleanly decide which interval to drop. The clean greedy needs end-time ordering, plus the trap of counting removals directly instead of keepers.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Reframe to 'maximize non-overlapping count', justify why earliest-finish is the optimal greedy (exchange argument), and note the start-sort variant works too if you delete the later-ending interval on conflict.

problemStatement:
Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [startᵢ, endᵢ]`, return the **minimum number of intervals you need to remove** to make the rest of the intervals non-overlapping.

Intervals that only touch at a point, like `[1,2]` and `[2,3]`, are considered **non-overlapping** — you do not need to remove either.
constraints: An interval always has start < end (no zero-length intervals)
understanding: You want to throw away as few intervals as possible so the survivors don't overlap. Equivalently — and more usefully — you want to keep as MANY non-overlapping intervals as possible. Once you've found the maximum keepable set, the removals are just everything else.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do touching intervals count as overlapping?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — [1,2] and [2,3] are fine and both can stay. That means the 'compatible' test is start >= prevEnd (with >=, not strict >).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I return the removed intervals or just the count?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the count of removals. Internally I'll count keepers and subtract from n.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the input sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. I'll sort it — by END time, which is the crux of the greedy.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can two intervals be identical?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Identical intervals overlap each other, so all but one must be removed — the greedy handles that naturally.

examples.explanation: Remove [1,3] and the rest ([1,2],[2,3],[3,4]) are non-overlapping. One removal.
All three are identical and mutually overlapping. Keep one, remove two.
They only touch at 2 — non-overlapping. Remove nothing.

approaches.name: Sort by Start + DP (Longest Non-overlapping Chain)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as the 'safe DP' if you don't yet trust the greedy — then point out it's O(n²) and the greedy beats it.
hints: Reframe: keep the most non-overlapping intervals, then removals = n − kept. Does that look like a known sequence problem?
Sort by start. Let dp[i] = the largest non-overlapping set ending with interval i. It's Longest Increasing Subsequence on intervals.
dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over all j < i where intervals[j].end <= intervals[i].start. The answer is n − max(dp).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Filling each dp[i] scans all earlier j, so n × n = O(n²). The greedy replaces this whole table with a single counter.
approaches.explanation:
Recast the problem as 'find the maximum set of mutually non-overlapping intervals', which is exactly a Longest Increasing Subsequence over intervals ordered by start.

**The DP recurrence.** Sort by start. Define `dp[i]` as the size of the largest compatible chain whose last interval is `i`. For each `i`, look at every earlier `j` whose end is ≤ interval `i`'s start (so they don't overlap) and take the best: `dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j])`. The biggest `dp[i]` is the maximum number you can keep, so the answer is `n − max(dp)`.

**Why it's correct but heavy.** This is the brute-force-but-principled way to compute the max keep set — it never assumes anything clever, just tries all chains. The cost is the nested scan: O(n²). For n up to 10⁵ that's 10¹⁰ operations — far too slow. It's worth stating to show you see the problem's structure, then immediately reach for the greedy that computes the same maximum in one pass.
approaches.insight: Seeing the problem as 'max chain of compatible intervals = LIS' is genuinely useful — it explains *why* the answer is n − (something maximized). The greedy is just a much faster way to find that same maximum, exploiting the special structure that LIS-in-general doesn't have.

dryRun.intro: dp[i] = longest compatible chain ending at i. Answer = n − max(dp).

java.explanation: j is compatible with i when j ends at or before i starts (touching allowed).
Extend the best compatible chain ending at j by interval i.

python.explanation: Non-overlap test — earlier interval finishes by the time i begins.
Removals = total minus the largest keepable chain.

edgeCases.behavior: No interval is compatible with another (all overlap); every dp[i]=1, best=1 → 3 − 1 = 2 removals.

pitfalls: O(n²) is far too slow for n = 10⁵ — only present this as a stepping stone.
Using strict `<` for compatibility wrongly treats touching intervals as overlapping.
Forgetting to subtract from n — the DP gives keepers, the answer is removals.

approaches.name: Greedy — Sort by End, Keep Earliest-Finishing (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Lead with 'this is activity selection: sort by end and greedily keep the earliest finisher'.
hints: If you could keep only one interval to leave maximum room for others, which would you pick?
Sort by END time. Greedily keep an interval whenever its start is ≥ the end of the last interval you kept.
Count keepers as you go; the answer is n − keepers. The earliest-finishing choice is provably optimal (exchange argument).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting by end is O(n log n) and dominates; one linear scan with a running prevEnd and counter is O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Sort the intervals by **end** time, then sweep once. Track `prevEnd` (the end of the last interval we decided to keep) and a `kept` counter. For each interval, if its start is `>= prevEnd` it doesn't conflict with anything we've kept, so keep it: increment `kept` and set `prevEnd` to this interval's end. Otherwise it overlaps a kept interval — 'remove' it by simply doing nothing. The answer is `n − kept`.

**Why sort by END, not start.** This is the activity-selection insight. Among intervals competing for the same slice of time, the one that *finishes earliest* leaves the most room for everything after it. So greedily committing to the earliest-finishing compatible interval is never a mistake — any other choice ends at least as late and can only block more future intervals. Sorting by end puts the earliest finisher first at every decision point, so a single forward scan makes the optimal choice each time.

**Why removing the later-finisher on conflict is safe.** When the current interval starts before `prevEnd`, two intervals fight for overlapping time. We already kept the one that ends earlier (it came first in end-order), so we discard the current (later-ending) one. Dropping the later finisher can only help future intervals, never hurt them — that's the exchange argument that proves the greedy optimal.

**Why count keepers, not removals.** Counting removals directly forces you to reason about *which* overlapper to drop in a cluster, which is fiddly. Counting keepers is a clean invariant — 'is this compatible with the last survivor?' — and `removals = n − kept` falls out for free.
approaches.insight: Earliest-finish-first is the single most reusable greedy in interval scheduling: it's correct precisely because finishing early dominates finishing late (it never closes off more options). Recognize 'maximize compatible intervals' or 'minimize removals to make disjoint' and your hand should reach for sort-by-end before you finish reading the prompt.

java.explanation: Sort by END — the earliest finisher comes first at every decision.
Compatible with the last survivor (touching allowed) → keep it.

python.explanation: End-time order is what makes greedy keeping optimal.
No conflict with the last kept interval → it's a survivor.
Removals = total − survivors; never count removals directly.

diagrams.caption: Sorted by end. Highlight = kept survivor; dim = removed overlapper. prevEnd only advances on a keep.

pitfalls: Sorting by start instead of end — the greedy choice is no longer obviously optimal.
Using strict `>` for the keep test — wrongly removes a touching, non-overlapping interval.
Counting removals directly inside the loop instead of n − kept — error-prone in clusters.

commonMistakes: Sorting by start instead of end, breaking the greedy.
Using strict > so touching intervals like [1,2] and [2,3] are wrongly treated as overlapping.
Returning the keeper count instead of n − keepers (the removals).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sorting by start instead of end
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The greedy 'keep earliest finisher' is optimal only when you process by end time. Sorting by start leaves you unable to cleanly decide which overlapper to drop.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: intervals.sort(key=lambda iv: iv[0])   # by start — wrong greedy
commonMistakesDetailed.good: intervals.sort(key=lambda iv: iv[1])   # by end — activity selection

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Treating touching intervals as overlapping
commonMistakesDetailed.why: [1,2] and [2,3] are non-overlapping for this problem. Using strict > in the keep test removes one of them needlessly and overcounts removals.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if s > prev_end:        # rejects a valid touching interval
    kept += 1; prev_end = e
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if s >= prev_end:       # touching is allowed
    kept += 1; prev_end = e

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning keepers instead of removals
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The greedy naturally counts survivors. The question asks for the number removed, so you must subtract from n.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return kept;                       // that's survivors, not removals
